title: The Waxhaws to the Garden Tomb: Old Hickory, the Removal, and the War on the Bank
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Waxhaws and the War That Takes His Family

stops.name: Waxhaws, the cabin on a line nobody has surveyed
stops.date_confidence: attested as to date; the state of birth is genuinely disputed, both Carolinas claim the cabin and no contemporary record fixes it
stops.campa: A son is born to a Scots-Irish widow in the Waxhaws, a settlement lying across a boundary no surveyor has yet run through the backcountry. His father died three weeks before and lies in the churchyard at Old Waxhaw; Elizabeth Hutchinson Jackson gives the child his name. South Carolina and North Carolina will each claim the cabin for two centuries, and neither will produce a contemporary paper that settles it. The boy is raised where the nearest court is a day's ride and where quarrels are settled by the men standing in the road.
suggested_refs: Andrew Jackson State Park, Lancaster County, South Carolina, the conventional marker for a birthplace no document fixes
Old Waxhaw Presbyterian Church cemetery, burial place of Andrew Jackson Sr.
sources: Miller Center, 'Andrew Jackson: Life in Brief'

stops.name: Stono Ferry, the first brother
stops.campa: Hugh Jackson marches with the militia to the Stono river below Charleston and dies of heat exhaustion after the action, the family's first loss to the Revolution. The attack that morning is an American one, thrown at a British force dug in above the ferry, and it fails. Andrew is twelve and stays in the Waxhaws with Robert and their mother while the British columns work north out of Savannah. The war has two more years to run in the Carolinas, and it takes Robert and Elizabeth both before it is finished with the house.
suggested_refs: The Stono Ferry battlefield at Rantowles, South Carolina, 20 June 1779
sources: Remini, Andrew Jackson and the Course of American Empire, vol. 1 (cited secondhand)

stops.name: The Crawford house, the officer's boots
stops.date_confidence: attested by Jackson's own later testimony, recorded by Parton and corroborated by Remini; the day within April is not recorded
stops.campa: British dragoons take Andrew and Robert at a relative's farmhouse in the Waxhaws. An officer orders the younger boy to clean his boots. Andrew answers that he is a prisoner of war and expects the treatment of one, and the officer swings his saber; the blade opens his scalp and lays his left hand to the bone. He carries both scars for the remaining sixty-four years of his life, and he tells the story to biographers and to visitors who come out to the Hermitage to hear it told.
suggested_refs: The Crawford farmhouse site in the Waxhaws, where Jackson took the saber cut
sources: James Parton, Life of Andrew Jackson (1860), recording Jackson's own account
Remini, Andrew Jackson and the Course of American Empire, vol. 1 (cited secondhand)

stops.name: Camden gaol, the smallpox
stops.date_confidence: attested as to event and month; the day is not recorded
stops.campa: The brothers are marched some forty miles to Camden and held in a crowded jail with the other prisoners. Both take smallpox there. Elizabeth Jackson walks to Camden and arranges an exchange, and the three of them start home on two horses, Robert on one and their mother on the other, Andrew on foot in the rain. Robert dies within days of reaching the Waxhaws. Andrew lies delirious for weeks in a house that now holds two people, and recovers into a war his family has already lost twice.
suggested_refs: The Camden gaol, South Carolina, where Robert Jackson contracted the smallpox that killed him
sources: Remini, Andrew Jackson and the Course of American Empire, vol. 1 (cited secondhand)

stops.name: Charleston harbour, the grave nobody marks
stops.date_confidence: attested as to month; the cause is given variously as cholera and as ship fever, and the sources do not agree. The Carrickfergus legacy and its loss at Charleston are tradition out of Parton and Remini, with no primary accounting, and are placed here out of strict sequence
stops.campa: Elizabeth Jackson travels to Charleston to nurse American prisoners held on the British ships in the harbour and dies of the fever she went to treat. She is buried in an unmarked plot outside the town and no search afterward recovers it. Her son is fourteen and has nobody left, and no property beyond a small inheritance from his grandfather in Ireland, which he will take to Charleston and spend there on horses and cards. Everything he holds afterward he takes for himself. There is no grave for him to visit.
suggested_refs: The Charleston prison ships of 1781 and the unlocated grave of Elizabeth Hutchinson Jackson
sources: Remini, Andrew Jackson and the Course of American Empire, vol. 1 (cited secondhand)
James Parton, Life of Andrew Jackson (1860), for the Carrickfergus legacy

stops.name: Salisbury, reading law in Rowan County
stops.date_confidence: attested as a period, 1784 to 1787; the arrival is not dated, and the day and month here are placeholders
stops.campa: He comes to Salisbury and reads law in the office of Spruce Macay, then with Colonel John Stokes, in the ordinary apprenticeship of the frontier bar. Salisbury remembers him for the horses, the cards, and the tavern fights as clearly as for the books. In September 1787 he is admitted to the North Carolina bar, twenty years old, holding a licence, a horse, a brace of pistols, and no family and no land at all. The licence is the only thing he owns that can carry him west.
suggested_refs: The law office of Spruce Macay, Salisbury, North Carolina
sources: Remini, Andrew Jackson and the Course of American Empire, vol. 1 (cited secondhand)

stops.name: Fort Nashborough, the prosecutor comes down the road
stops.campa: He practises briefly at Jonesborough, then rides to the settlement on the Cumberland to take up the post of public prosecutor for the Western District of North Carolina. The Southwest Territory does not exist yet and will not be created for two more years. Nashville is a stockade with a few hundred people around it. He boards in the house of the widow Donelson, where a daughter named Rachel is living apart from her husband, and begins collecting debts for creditors at a rate that makes him a fortune and a set of enemies.
suggested_refs: Fort Nashborough on the Cumberland, the settlement Jackson reached in October 1788
sources: Remini, Andrew Jackson and the Course of American Empire, vol. 1 (cited secondhand)

stops.name: Springfield Plantation, the marriage that leaves no record
stops.date_confidence: tradition only; no documentary evidence of an 1791 ceremony has been produced, at this house or anywhere else. The documented ceremony is at Nashville in January 1794
stops.campa: The house tradition of a plantation near Fayette holds that Andrew Jackson marries Rachel Donelson Robards here, believing her divorce from Lewis Robards final. It is not final. No paper recording any 1791 ceremony has ever been produced, at this house or at any other. What exists on paper is a second ceremony at Nashville in January 1794, after the decree actually clears. The gap between the two dates, whatever it contains, is handed to his enemies and used against Rachel until the week she dies.
suggested_refs: Springfield Plantation, Fayette, Mississippi, whose marriage tradition no document supports
The January 1794 Nashville marriage bond, the documented ceremony
sources: Miller Center, 'Andrew Jackson: Life in Brief'

stops.name: Philadelphia, the first seat Tennessee sends
stops.campa: Tennessee enters the Union and sends him to Congress as its first Representative. He takes his seat in the capital where Thomas Jefferson is arriving as Vice President and where Jefferson has already fought Alexander Hamilton to a standstill over a national bank, and he votes against the resolution thanking George Washington on his retirement. He is twenty-nine. He stays a year, moves up to the Senate, and resigns that in 1798 for a judgeship at home. He returns to Hamilton's argument thirty-six years later, holding a veto.
stops.quote: Alexander Hamilton, whose bank, whose funding scheme, and whose admiration for the English constitution look to Jefferson like a monarchy assembling itself out of paper.
stops.quote_source: thomas_jefferson.journey.json, stop 'Philadelphia, the quarrel with Hamilton'
suggested_refs: Congress Hall, Philadelphia, seat of the federal government from 1790 to 1800
The First Bank of the United States on Third Street, chartered 1791, expired 1811
sources: Miller Center, 'Andrew Jackson: Life in Brief'

stops.name: The Hermitage, the tract on the Cumberland
stops.date_confidence: attested as the year of purchase; the day and month are placeholders
stops.campa: He buys a farm in Davidson County and calls it the Hermitage: cotton, horses, a store, a racetrack, and a log house he will replace in brick. The place is worked by enslaved people, nine at the start and more than a hundred by the time he dies in it. He breeds racehorses and quarrels about them, and two years after the purchase one of those quarrels kills a man and puts a bullet in his chest. The militia rank and the standing among planters come with the land.
suggested_refs: The Hermitage, Davidson County, Tennessee, and the quarters of the people enslaved there
sources: The Hermitage (Andrew Jackson Foundation), site history
Remini, Andrew Jackson and the Course of American Empire, vol. 1 (cited secondhand)

stops.name: The Red River, the duel with Dickinson
stops.campa: Charles Dickinson, the best pistol shot in Tennessee, has insulted Rachel in print over a horse-racing wager. They meet across the Kentucky line because Tennessee has outlawed duelling. Jackson lets Dickinson fire first; the ball breaks two ribs and lodges beside his heart. He stands, takes aim, and kills him. The bullet is never taken out. It is still in him thirty-nine years later at the Hermitage, when the doctors set it down on the list of things that are killing him.
suggested_refs: The duelling ground on the Red River near Adairville, Logan County, Kentucky
sources: Remini, Andrew Jackson and the Course of American Empire, vol. 1 (cited secondhand)

stops.name: Fort Mims, the stockade in the canebrake
stops.campa: Creek Red Sticks take the stockade at Fort Mims in the Tensaw country and kill several hundred settlers, mixed-blood Creeks, and enslaved people inside it. The Creek Nation is already at civil war with itself, and the Red Sticks are the faction that has broken with the accommodationists; the killing at Fort Mims is an act in that war. The United States reads it as an act in a different war. Tennessee votes money and men, and Jackson, in bed in Nashville with a shattered shoulder, takes the field.
suggested_refs: Fort Mims Historic Site, Tensaw, Baldwin County, Alabama
sources: Alabama Historical Commission, Fort Mims Historic Site
Remini, Andrew Jackson and the Course of American Empire, vol. 1 (cited secondhand)

stops.name: The City Hotel, a gun battle in the street
stops.campa: Five days after Fort Mims, Jackson and John Coffee meet Thomas Hart Benton and his brother Jesse outside the City Hotel in Nashville over a quarrel about somebody else's duel. Pistols and knives come out in the corridor and on the sidewalk. Jackson takes a ball in the left shoulder that nearly costs him the arm and is not fully removed for nineteen years. Twenty-four years after that, Thomas Hart Benton stands on the Senate floor and moves to strike Jackson's censure out of the record.
suggested_refs: The City Hotel, Nashville, site of the Jackson-Benton affray of 4 September 1813
sources: Remini, Andrew Jackson and the Course of American Empire, vol. 1 (cited secondhand)

stops.name: Tallushatchee, the child taken from the dead
stops.campa: Coffee's detachment surrounds the Creek town of Tallushatchee and destroys it, killing some hundred and eighty-six warriors. Among the dead a nursing infant is found alive beside his mother. The Creek survivors, who have nothing, refuse to take him. Jackson sends the child to the Hermitage, names him Lyncoya, and raises him in the house until he dies of tuberculosis at sixteen. The same campaign produces the treaty that takes the Creek Nation's land, including the land of the Creeks who fight on Jackson's side.
suggested_refs: The site of Tallushatchee near Alexandria, Calhoun County, Alabama
Lyncoya Jackson, raised at the Hermitage, died 1828
sources: Remini, Andrew Jackson and the Course of American Empire, vol. 1 (cited secondhand)

stops.name: Horseshoe Bend, the bend in the Tallapoosa
stops.campa: The Red Sticks fortify the neck of a horseshoe bend of the Tallapoosa with a log barricade and hold the town of Tohopeka behind it, with the river on three sides. Jackson's force, which includes Cherokee and allied Creek fighters, crosses the water below, fires the town from behind, and storms the barricade. Over eight hundred Red Stick warriors are killed in the bend and in the river. It ends Creek military power in the Southeast, and it makes Jackson, at forty-seven, a general the War Department cannot ignore.
suggested_refs: Horseshoe Bend National Military Park, Tallapoosa County, Alabama
sources: National Park Service, Horseshoe Bend National Military Park

stops.name: Fort Jackson, the treaty the allies also sign
stops.date_confidence: attested; the size of the cession is given as 23 million acres by Remini and as over 20 million by Wikipedia and history.state.gov, and the sources are not reconciled here
stops.campa: At the confluence of the Coosa and the Tallapoosa he dictates terms to the Creek Nation. The cession runs to twenty or twenty-three million acres depending on which account is read, roughly half of present Alabama with a piece of Georgia. It is taken from the whole nation, including the Creeks who fought beside him at Horseshoe Bend, on the argument that a nation is answerable as a body for a war fought by part of it. The principle is stated here first and applied for the next twenty-five years.
suggested_refs: Fort Toulouse-Fort Jackson Park at the Coosa and Tallapoosa confluence, near Wetumpka, Alabama
The Treaty of Fort Jackson, 9 August 1814, National Archives text
sources: National Archives, Treaty of Fort Jackson
Remini, Andrew Jackson and the Course of American Empire, vol. 1 (cited secondhand)

stops.name: Pensacola, the port taken without orders
stops.campa: Spain is neutral and Pensacola is Spanish, and a British force is using the harbour and arming Creeks and Seminoles out of it. Jackson has no authorization from Washington. He marches on the town, storms it in a morning, watches the British blow the fort at Barrancas and sail, and then leaves. The administration is embarrassed and does not discipline him. Four years later he crosses the same border into Spanish territory again, and again without an order to do it.
suggested_refs: Pensacola and Fort San Carlos de Barrancas, Spanish Florida, November 1814
sources: Remini, Andrew Jackson and the Course of American Empire, vol. 1 (cited secondhand)

stops.name: New Orleans, the city under martial law
stops.campa: He reaches New Orleans and finds a city of French and Spanish creoles, Americans, free men of colour, and smugglers, none of whom trust each other and few of whom trust him. He puts the whole of it under martial law. Into his line he takes regulars, militia, two battalions of free men of colour, Choctaw fighters, and Jean Lafitte's Baratarian gunners, whom the United States has been prosecuting as pirates. John Cleves Symmes, garrisoned in this same southern theatre and made captain of infantry the year before, serves the war Jackson is about to end.
suggested_refs: Jackson's martial-law proclamation at New Orleans, 16 December 1814
sources: Remini, Andrew Jackson and the Course of American Empire, vol. 1 (cited secondhand)
symmes.journey.json, stop 'New Orleans, the southern garrison'

stops.name: Chalmette, the morning below the city
stops.campa: The British advance in the fog across cane stubble toward a mud rampart and a canal, into artillery laid to enfilade the field and rifles firing in ranks from behind cover. It is over in half an hour. Two hundred and ninety-one British soldiers are killed and better than two thousand counted killed, wounded, or taken; seventy-one Americans are casualties, thirteen of them dead. The Treaty of Ghent ended the war a fortnight earlier and nobody on the field knows it. The country hears of the victory first and the peace second, and never separates them again.
suggested_refs: Chalmette Battlefield, Jean Lafitte National Historical Park, Louisiana

stops.name: San Marcos de Apalache, two Britons hanged
stops.campa: Sent to pursue Seminole raiders across the border, he takes the Spanish fort at St. Marks instead. He arrests two British subjects, the trader Alexander Arbuthnot and the former marine Robert Ambrister, tries them before a court of his own officers for aiding the Seminoles, and has Arbuthnot hanged from the yardarm of his own ship and Ambrister shot. Two governments protest. John Quincy Adams, alone in the cabinet, defends him, and turns the incident into the argument that Spain cannot hold Florida.
suggested_refs: San Marcos de Apalache Historic State Park, St. Marks, Florida
sources: Florida Division of Historical Resources, San Marcos de Apalache
Miller Center, 'Andrew Jackson: Life in Brief'

stops.name: Pensacola again, and then the flag comes down
stops.campa: He occupies Pensacola a second time on his own authority, deposes the Spanish governor, and installs one of his own colonels in the office. Congress opens an inquiry into censuring him and does not censure him. Spain, unable to garrison the province and unable to expel him from it, signs the Adams-Onis Treaty the following year and cedes Florida. In 1821 Jackson comes back as the territory's first American governor, quarrels with nearly everyone in it, and resigns inside three months.
suggested_refs: The Adams-Onis Treaty of 1819 and the Florida transfer of 1821
sources: Miller Center, 'Andrew Jackson: Life in Brief'
Remini, Andrew Jackson and the Course of American Empire, vol. 1 (cited secondhand)

stops.name: Washington, the general takes a Senate seat
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year; the day of taking his seat is not fixed here
stops.campa: Tennessee sends him back to the Senate twenty-five years after he resigned from it, this time as the most famous soldier in the country and a candidate for the presidency in everything but name. He is fifty-six. He makes a point of reconciling in public with Thomas Hart Benton, now a senator himself, whose brother put a ball in Jackson's shoulder in a Nashville street. The seat is a platform rather than an office, and nobody in the chamber mistakes it for one.
suggested_refs: Jackson's second term in the United States Senate, 1823 to 1825
sources: Miller Center, 'Andrew Jackson: Life in Brief'

stops.name: The Capitol, the House chooses Adams
stops.campa: Four candidates split the field and nobody holds a majority, though Jackson leads in the popular vote and in the electoral college both. The choice falls to the House. Henry Clay, eliminated and holding the votes that decide it, gives them to John Quincy Adams, and Adams makes Clay his Secretary of State within days. Jackson resigns his Senate seat, goes home to Tennessee, and campaigns for four years on two words. The corrupt bargain is never proved and never needs to be.
suggested_refs: The contingent presidential election in the House of Representatives, 9 February 1825
sources: Miller Center, 'Andrew Jackson: Life in Brief'

stops.name: The Hermitage, Rachel does not go to Washington
stops.campa: He wins the rematch in a campaign that prints the 1791 marriage in every opposition paper in the country and calls her an adulteress in type. She reads some of it. Weeks after the election and weeks before he is to leave for the capital, she dies at the Hermitage of a heart attack and is buried in the garden in the white dress bought for the inauguration. He holds his political enemies responsible for her death for the remaining seventeen years of his life, and never remarries.
suggested_refs: The garden tomb at the Hermitage, built for Rachel Jackson in 1831
sources: The Hermitage (Andrew Jackson Foundation), site history

stops.name: The Capitol, and then the crowd gets into the house
stops.campa: He takes the oath on the East Portico in mourning black, a widower of ten weeks, and reads an inaugural address most of the crowd cannot hear. The crowd follows him to the White House reception, comes in through the windows, stands on the furniture in muddy boots, and breaks the china; the punch is carried out onto the lawn to draw them off. His opponents call it the reign of King Mob. He governs afterward through an informal circle the press names the Kitchen Cabinet, and through an official cabinet the Eaton affair is already pulling apart.
suggested_refs: The East Portico of the Capitol, 4 March 1829, and the White House reception that followed
sources: Miller Center, 'Andrew Jackson: Life in Brief'
Remini, Andrew Jackson and the Course of American Empire, vol. 2 (cited secondhand)

stops.name: The Capitol, the Indian Removal Act
stops.campa: The bill passes the House by five votes and he signs it. It authorizes the president to negotiate the exchange of tribal land east of the Mississippi for territory west of it, and it is written in the language of exchange from beginning to end: nothing in it compels anyone to move. He tells Congress the policy protects the Southeastern nations from the states that are dismantling them. Nearly seventy removal treaties follow. Every forced march of the next decade rests on this sheet of paper.
suggested_refs: The Indian Removal Act of 1830, original act text, National Archives
sources: National Archives, Indian Removal Act of 1830

stops.name: Dancing Rabbit Creek, the first treaty under the act
stops.campa: Choctaw leaders sign away the last Choctaw land in Mississippi four months after the act, the first nation to go. The treaty carries a clause letting families stay as citizens of Mississippi on individual allotments, and the state and the registrars between them make the clause nearly impossible to use. Some thirteen thousand Choctaw walk west over the following three years, through winter and cholera. A faction signs under pressure supplied by the state, and the federal government supplies the escort afterward.
suggested_refs: The Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek, Noxubee County, Mississippi, 27 September 1830
sources: National Archives, Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek

stops.name: Washington, the Court rules and nothing happens
stops.campa: The Marshall Court holds in Worcester v. Georgia that the Cherokee Nation is a distinct community within which the laws of Georgia have no force, moving off the ground it took a year earlier in Cherokee Nation v. Georgia. Georgia ignores the ruling. Jackson declines to enforce it. The line the schoolbooks hand him, that John Marshall has made his decision and now let him enforce it, is in no contemporary record and is almost certainly not his; the non-enforcement is entirely his and nobody disputes it.
suggested_refs: Worcester v. Georgia, 31 U.S. 515 (1832), and the missionaries imprisoned at Milledgeville

stops.name: New Echota, twenty men sign for a nation
stops.campa: A faction of some twenty Cherokee, holding no authority from the national council, signs away every acre of Cherokee land east of the Mississippi for five million dollars and territory in the west. Principal Chief John Ross is not present and does not consent; he brings the Senate a protest carrying nearly sixteen thousand Cherokee signatures, which is most of the nation. The Senate ratifies the treaty in May 1836 by a single vote. Several of the signers are killed by their own people four years later in Indian Territory.
suggested_refs: New Echota Historic Site, Gordon County, Georgia
The Treaty of New Echota, 29 December 1835, National Archives text
sources: National Archives, Treaty of New Echota
National Park Service, Trail of Tears National Historic Trail

stops.name: Ross's Landing, the stockades on the river
stops.campa: Fifteen months after the treaty deadline, Winfield Scott's soldiers take the Cherokee out of their houses at bayonet point and hold them in stockades on the Tennessee River before loading them west. Roughly four thousand die on the road and in the camps by the standard estimate, and published ranges run higher. Jackson has been out of office fifteen months and is at the Hermitage. Fifty years on, the same War Department marches Sitting Bull and Low Dog off the Northern Plains to agencies, under the same statute-and-escort machinery this river landing is running now.
stops.quote: Now, I want to learn the white man's way, for I see that he is stronger than we are, and that his government is better than ours.
stops.quote_source: Low Dog, account printed at Leavenworth, Kansas, 18 August 1881; carried in low_dog.journey.json
suggested_refs: Ross's Landing, Chattanooga, one of three emigration depots of the 1838 removal
The Trail of Tears National Historic Trail, nine states
sources: National Park Service, Trail of Tears National Historic Trail

stops.name: The White House, the veto
stops.campa: Nicholas Biddle, with Clay and Webster behind him, pushes a recharter of the Second Bank of the United States through Congress four years early, to force the question into an election year. Jackson returns the bill to the Senate with a message that does not argue the Bank is badly run. It argues that the Bank is unconstitutional whatever the Supreme Court said in 1819, that a fifth of its stock is held abroad, and that exclusive privilege granted by government is taken from everyone outside the grant. The message is written for voters rather than for senators, and on voters it works.
stops.quote: It is to be regretted that the rich and powerful too often bend the acts of government to their selfish purposes.
stops.quote_source: Andrew Jackson, Bank Veto Message, 10 July 1832 (Avalon Project, Yale Law School)
suggested_refs: The Bank Veto Message of 10 July 1832, full text, Avalon Project
sources: Avalon Project, Yale Law School, Bank Veto Message, 10 July 1832

stops.name: Columbia, the state declares the tariff void
stops.campa: Three weeks after Jackson is reelected by a wide margin, a South Carolina convention declares the federal tariffs null within the state and threatens secession if they are collected at Charleston. John C. Calhoun, his own first Vice President, resigns the vice presidency to lead the nullifiers from the Senate. Jackson issues a proclamation denying that any state may leave the Union, asks Congress for authority to use the army, and is given it. The state suspends its ordinance after a compromise tariff, and both sides claim the settlement.
suggested_refs: The South Carolina Ordinance of Nullification, 24 November 1832, and Jackson's Nullification Proclamation of 10 December
sources: South Carolina Department of Archives and History
Remini, Andrew Jackson and the Course of American Empire, vol. 2 (cited secondhand)

stops.name: The White House, the deposits
stops.date_confidence: attested as the day he read the removal paper to the cabinet; the removals themselves begin 1 October 1833
stops.campa: Reading the election as a mandate, he reads the cabinet a paper announcing that federal revenue will no longer be deposited in the Second Bank and that what is there will be drawn down. William Duane, his Treasury Secretary, refuses to sign the order and is dismissed on 22 September; Roger Taney is appointed the next day and signs it; removals begin on 1 October. The money goes to selected state banks, seven at first and past thirty within a few years, which the opposition names the pet banks. Taney is the fourth man to hold the Treasury under him in four years.
stops.quote: I have now done my duty to my country. If sustained by my fellow citizens, I shall be grateful and happy; if not, I shall find in the motives which impel me ample grounds for contentment and peace.
stops.quote_source: Andrew Jackson, Bank Veto Message, 10 July 1832 (Avalon Project, Yale Law School), near the close
suggested_refs: Girard Bank, Third and Chestnut Streets, Philadelphia, among the first of the deposit banks
sources: Wikipedia, 'United States Secretary of the Treasury'
Remini, Andrew Jackson and the Bank War (cited secondhand)

stops.name: Chestnut Street, Biddle answers
stops.date_confidence: attested as a period running through the winter of 1833 to 1834; the day is a placeholder
stops.campa: From the marble bank on Chestnut Street, Biddle answers the removals by calling in loans and contracting credit across the country, on the reasoning that a hard enough squeeze brings Congress to him with a recharter in its hands. Businesses fail through the winter and delegations of merchants come to Washington to ask Jackson for relief. He tells them to go to Biddle. Contemporaries call it Biddle's panic. The Bank has shown in public that it can make money scarce whenever it chooses, which is the thing the veto message accused it of.
stops.quote: From its superior strength it could seriously injure, if not destroy, the business of any one of them which might incur its resentment; and it openly claimed for itself the power of regulating the currency throughout the United States.
stops.quote_source: Andrew Jackson, Farewell Address, 4 March 1837 (Miller Center, University of Virginia), on the Second Bank
suggested_refs: The Second Bank of the United States, Chestnut Street, Philadelphia, now part of Independence National Historical Park
sources: Remini, Andrew Jackson and the Bank War (cited secondhand)
Charles Sellers, The Market Revolution (cited secondhand)

stops.name: The Senate chamber, the censure
stops.campa: Henry Clay carries a resolution declaring that the President has assumed upon himself authority not conferred by the Constitution and the laws. It is the first censure of a sitting president. Jackson sends the Senate a protest calling the vote itself unconstitutional, on the ground that the chamber has convicted him of an offence with no impeachment before it, and the Senate refuses to enter his protest in the journal. Thomas Hart Benton rises the same session, gives notice that he will move to expunge the censure, and gives that notice again every year afterward.
suggested_refs: United States Senate Historical Office, 'Censure of President Andrew Jackson'

stops.name: The Treasury, the debt at zero
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the month the debt was extinguished; the anniversary date is used here and no act of Congress marks it
stops.campa: On the twentieth anniversary of New Orleans, the United States owes nothing. No act of Congress does it. The debt is retired out of surplus, out of tariff revenue and above all out of the money pouring in from public land sales in the west, the same boom the pet banks are lending into. It has never happened before and it does not happen again in the history of the republic. He counts it, alongside the destruction of the Bank, as the work of his presidency. Within two years the land bubble the surplus rests on breaks and takes the deposit banks down with it.
suggested_refs: The extinction of the United States national debt, January 1835, the only occasion in the nation's history

stops.name: The Capitol, two pistols that do not fire
stops.campa: Leaving a funeral in the House chamber, Jackson is met in the rotunda by Richard Lawrence, an unemployed house painter who believes himself the rightful king of England. Lawrence fires a pistol at him from a few paces; the cap detonates and the charge does not. He draws a second pistol and that one misfires as well. Jackson, sixty-seven years old and in mourning dress, goes at him with his cane and has to be pulled off him. It is the first attempt on the life of an American president.
suggested_refs: The Richard Lawrence assassination attempt, Capitol rotunda, 30 January 1835

stops.name: The Treasury, gold or silver only
stops.campa: Speculators are buying federal land with banknotes issued by the same banks that hold the federal deposits, borrowing the paper into existence and paying the government back with it. The Specie Circular orders the land offices to take nothing but gold and silver. Paper falls, specie moves west out of the eastern banks to meet the demand, and the credit carrying the boom begins to unwind. Whether the circular or the movement of British bullion breaks the country the following year is argued to this day.
stops.quote: The Constitution of the United States unquestionably intended to secure to the people a circulating medium of gold and silver.
stops.quote_source: Andrew Jackson, Farewell Address, 4 March 1837 (Miller Center, University of Virginia)
suggested_refs: The Specie Circular of 11 July 1836, National Archives text
sources: Peter Temin on the causes of the Panic of 1837 (cited secondhand)

stops.name: The Senate chamber, black lines through the record
stops.campa: After three years of moving it and losing, Thomas Hart Benton carries the expunging resolution at last, in a Senate remade by Jackson's own elections. The Secretary of the Senate takes down the manuscript journal of 1834, draws black lines around the censure, and writes across it that it has been expunged by order of the Senate. Clay and Webster protest in the chamber while the ink goes on. The brother of the man who shot Jackson in a Nashville street in 1813 has taken the sentence off him.

stops.name: The Capitol, the Farewell Address
stops.campa: He leaves office on the day Martin Van Buren takes it, more popular than when he arrived, and publishes a farewell address that is largely about money. Forty years earlier, in Philadelphia, Hamilton drafted a farewell address for George Washington that defended the funding system; this one is the answer to it. He warns that a currency of paper concentrates power in a few hands, breeds speculation, and finds its way into the public councils. Six weeks later the banks of New York suspend specie payment.
stops.quote: The paper system being founded on public confidence and having of itself no intrinsic value, it is liable to great and sudden fluctuations, thereby rendering property insecure and the wages of labor unsteady and uncertain.
stops.quote_source: Andrew Jackson, Farewell Address, 4 March 1837 (Miller Center, University of Virginia)

stops.name: The Hermitage, the panic arrives
stops.campa: The New York banks suspend specie payment nine weeks after he leaves Washington, and the country enters six years of depression. His opponents name it after the Specie Circular and the Bank War; his defenders name it after British bullion and the price of cotton. He is at the Hermitage, out of office and short of money, home to a plantation his adopted son has mismanaged into debt. He spends the rest of his life defending the veto in letters to men who write to ask him about it.
stops.quote: It asserted (and it undoubtedly possessed) the power to make money plenty or scarce at its pleasure, at any time and in any quarter of the Union.
stops.quote_source: Andrew Jackson, Farewell Address, 4 March 1837 (Miller Center, University of Virginia), on the Second Bank

stops.name: The Hermitage, the garden tomb
stops.date_confidence: attested as to death; interment was two days later, on 10 June 1845, and the Hermitage pages were unreachable for a confirming lookup
stops.campa: He dies at the Hermitage of dropsy, heart failure, tuberculosis, and the two bullets he has carried since 1806 and 1813. He is seventy-eight. Two days later they bury him in the garden beside Rachel, under the domed limestone canopy he raised over her in 1831 and where she has lain since. The stone gives his name as General Andrew Jackson and stops there. It does not mention that he was President of the United States, and nobody has ever added it.

stops.name: Lafayette Square, the horse on two legs
stops.campa: Clark Mills, who has never seen an equestrian statue, casts one in bronze from British cannon Jackson captured, and balances the horse on its hind legs alone with nothing propping the tail. It is unveiled opposite the White House on the anniversary of New Orleans, the first equestrian bronze cast in the United States. Forty years later the square is completed with a standing Lafayette at one corner and Rochambeau, Kosciuszko, and von Steuben at the others: four foreign volunteers of the Revolution posted around the man that Revolution orphaned.
stops.quote: Andrew Jackson rides the middle of the square on his horse.
stops.quote_source: marques_de_lafayette.journey.json, stop 'Lafayette Square, Washington: the standing bronze'

stops.name: Jackson Square, the second cast
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year of dedication; the day and month are placeholders
stops.campa: The old Place d'Armes, where the city held its thanksgiving procession for him in January 1815, is renamed for him and takes the second cast of the Mills statue. A third goes to the Tennessee capitol grounds in 1880. In the twenty-first century the New Orleans bronze is defaced with paint and petitioned against on account of the Removal Act, and unlike the Confederate monuments the city took down in the same years, it is still standing on its plinth in the square that carries his name.

stops.name: The Bureau of Engraving, the face on the paper
stops.date_confidence: attested as the year the current portrait was introduced; the day and month are placeholders
stops.campa: The twenty-dollar note is redesigned and Jackson's portrait goes on the front of it, where it has stayed ever since. He killed a national bank on the argument that paper founded on public confidence has no intrinsic value of its own and leaves the wages of labour at the mercy of speculation. In 2016 the Treasury announces that Harriet Tubman will replace him on the face of the note; the plan is shelved, revived in 2021, and no such bill has been issued.
